heath_proof: For let the area ABCD be contained by the rationalstraight line AB and the second binomial AD; I say that the “side” of the area AC is a first bimedial straight line. For, since AD is a second binomial straight line, let it be divided into its terms at E, so that AE is the greater term;therefore AE, ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable with AE, and the lesser term ED is commensurable in length with AB. [X. Deff. II. 2] Let ED be bisected at F, and let there be applied to AE the rectangle AG, GE equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure; therefore AG is commensurable in length with GE. [X. 17] Through G, E, F let GH, EK, FL be drawn parallel toAB, CD, let the square SN be constructed equal to the parallelogram AH, and the square NQ equal to GK, and let them be placed so that MN is in a straight line with NO;therefore RN is also in a straight line with NP. Let the square SQ be completed. It is then manifest from what was proved before that MR is a mean proportional between SN, NQ and is equal to EL, and that MO is the “side” of the area AC. It is now to be proved that MO is a first bimedial straight line. Since AE is incommensurable in length with ED, while ED is commensurable with AB, therefore AE is incommensurable with AB. [X. 13] And, since AG is commensurable with EG,AE is also commensurable with each of the straight lines AG, GE. [X. 15] But AE is incommensurable in length with AB; therefore AG, GE are also incommensurable with AB. [X. 13] Therefore BA, AG and BA, GE are pairs of rationalstraight lines commensurable in square only; so that each of the rectangles AH, GK is medial. [X. 21] Hence each of the squares SN, NQ is medial. Therefore MN, NO are also medial. And, since AG is commensurable in length with GE,AH is also commensurable with GK, [VI. 1. X. 11] that is, SN is commensurable with NQ, that is, the square on MN with the square on NO. And, since AE is incommensurable in length with ED, while AE is commensurable with AG,and ED is commensurable with EF, therefore AG is incommensurable with EF; [X. 13] so that AH is also incommensurable with EL, that is, SN is incommensurable with MR, that is, PN with NR, [VI. 1, X. 11]that is, MN is incommensurable in length with NO. But MN, NO were proved to be both medial and commensurable in square; therefore MN, NO are medial straight lines commensurable in square only. I say next that they also contain a rational rectangle. For, since DE is, by hypothesis, commensurable with each of the straight lines AB, EF, therefore EF is also commensurable with EK. [X. 12] And each of them is rational;therefore EL, that is, MR is rational, [X. 19] and MR is the rectangle MN, NO. But, if two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational and is called a first bimedial straight line. [X. 37] Therefore MO is a first bimedial straight line.

10.55
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line which is called a first bimedial.

**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line which is called a first bimedial.

Notation: sq(X) denotes the square on X; rect(X, Y) denotes the rectangle contained by X, Y.

**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the second binomial AD, so that AC is the rectangle with adjacent sides AB, AD. Let AD be divided into its terms at E, AE being the greater term. Since AD is a binomial, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; and since AD is a second binomial, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and the lesser term ED is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB [D10.2.1, D10.2.2].

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10]. Since ED is cut at F, sq(ED) is equal to sq(EF), sq(FD) together with twice rect(EF, FD) [2.4]; and EF = FD, so sq(ED) is four times sq(EF), i.e. sq(EF) is the fourth part of sq(ED).

**Step 3.** Since AE is greater than ED, EF (the half of ED) is less than the half of AE, so that sq(EF) is less than the square on the half of AE. Therefore to AE there can be applied a parallelogram equal to sq(EF) and deficient by a square figure [6.28]. Let it be applied, cutting AE at G, the deficient square being described on GE; the applied parallelogram, having sides AG and GE, is rect(AG, GE), and thus rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF).

**Step 4.** Now sq(AE), the square on the greater of the two unequal straight lines AE, ED, exceeds sq(ED) by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and to AE has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of sq(ED) [Step 2] and deficient by a square figure, dividing AE into AG, GE; therefore AG and GE are commensurable in length [10.17].

**Step 5.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB, meeting BC at H, K, L [1.31]. Then AH, GK, EL, FC are rectangles, and the whole AC is made up of AH, GK, EL, FC. Their sides GH, EK, DC are each equal to AB [1.34], so AH = rect(AB, AG), GK = rect(AB, GE), EL = rect(AB, EF), FC = rect(AB, FD). Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC stand on equal bases and are in the same parallels AD, BC; therefore EL = FC [1.36].

**Step 6.** Since rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF), the three straight lines AG, EF, GE are proportional: AG : EF = EF : GE [6.17]. Also AH, EL, GK are parallelograms under the same height AB, so AH : EL = AG : EF and EL : GK = EF : GE [6.1].

**Step 7.** Let MN be the side of a square equal to AH [2.14], and to the three straight lines AG, EF, MN let NO be a fourth proportional, so that AG : EF = MN : NO [6.12]; and let NO be placed in a straight line with MN, so that MO is the straight line made up of MN and NO.

**Step 8.** The square on MN and the rectangle MN, NO are parallelograms under the same height MN on the bases MN, NO; therefore sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = MN : NO [6.1]. But MN : NO = AG : EF [Step 7] and AG : EF = AH : EL [Step 6]; therefore sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = AH : EL [5.11]. And sq(MN) = AH, so AH : rect(MN, NO) = AH : EL [5.7]; therefore rect(MN, NO) = EL [5.9].

**Step 9.** Likewise the rectangle MN, NO and the square on NO are parallelograms under the same height NO on the bases MN, NO; therefore rect(MN, NO) : sq(NO) = MN : NO [6.1]. But MN : NO = AG : EF = EF : GE = EL : GK [Steps 6, 7]; therefore rect(MN, NO) : sq(NO) = EL : GK [5.11]. And rect(MN, NO) = EL [Step 8], so EL : sq(NO) = EL : GK [5.7]; therefore sq(NO) = GK [5.9].

**Step 10.** Since MO is cut at N, sq(MO) is equal to sq(MN), sq(NO) together with twice rect(MN, NO) [2.4]. But sq(MN) = AH, sq(NO) = GK, and twice rect(MN, NO) equals EL together with FC [Steps 5, 8, 9]; so sq(MO) equals AH, GK, EL, FC together [CN2], that is, the whole AC [CN1]. Therefore MO is the "side" of the area AC [D10.1.4].

It remains to show that MO is a first bimedial.

**Step 11.** Since AG, GE are commensurable in length [Step 4], the whole AE is commensurable in length with each of AG, GE [10.15].

**Step 12.** Since AE, ED are commensurable in square only, AE is incommensurable in length with ED; but ED is commensurable in length with AB; therefore AE is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13]. And each of AG, GE is commensurable in length with AE [Step 11]; therefore each of AG, GE is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13].

**Step 13.** Since AG is commensurable in length with AE, sq(AG) has to sq(AE) the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; hence sq(AG), sq(AE) are commensurable [10.6]. And AE, being rational, is commensurable with AB in square, i.e. sq(AE), sq(AB) are commensurable [D10.1.3, D10.1.2]; therefore sq(AG), sq(AB) are commensurable [10.12], so that AG is commensurable in square with AB [D10.1.2] and hence rational [D10.1.3]. But AG is incommensurable in length with AB [Step 12]; hence AB, AG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. In the same way AB, GE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 14.** Therefore AH = rect(AB, AG) and GK = rect(AB, GE) are each contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so each is irrational and the side of the square equal to each is medial [10.21]. Since sq(MN) = AH and sq(NO) = GK, MN and NO are medial straight lines.

**Step 15.** AH : GK = AG : GE [6.1], and AG is commensurable with GE [Step 4]; therefore AH is commensurable with GK [10.11], that is, sq(MN) is commensurable with sq(NO); hence MN, NO are commensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 16.** Since ED is double of EF, EF measures ED, so ED and EF are commensurable [D10.1.1]; and ED is commensurable in length with AB; therefore EF is commensurable in length with AB [10.12]. But AG is incommensurable in length with AB [Step 12]; therefore AG is incommensurable in length with EF [10.13]. And AG : EF = MN : NO [Step 7]; therefore MN is incommensurable in length with NO [10.11]. Hence MN, NO are medial straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 17.** The rectangle MN, NO is equal to EL [Step 8], which is rect(AB, EF) [Step 5]. Now AB is rational, and EF, being commensurable in length with AB [Step 16], is rational [D10.1.3]; therefore rect(AB, EF) is rational [10.19], and so rect(MN, NO) is rational.

**Step 18.** Thus MN, NO are medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle; therefore the whole MO is irrational, namely the straight line called a first bimedial [10.37]. And MO is the side of the area AC [Step 10]. Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the side of the area is the irrational straight line called a first bimedial. Q.E.D.
